column1: # anchor|sequence|camera|English visual/action description|persistent end state

1|HOOK|wide tracking|At ground level, tiny workers brace their feet and try pushing a huge rough block; it barely shifts. Pull back to reveal its immense scale, without any modern machinery.|H1 block grounded; red worker at left edge; five companions behind him; no tools attached.

1:8|HOOK|close to wide|Hands strain against H1; its edge stays planted while dust compresses below it. Reveal the whole unsuccessful team, making the weight problem legible.|H1 remains grounded in its original position; same six workers relax their pushing stance.

2|HOOK|wide|Track along a massive stone wall, then settle on H1 and the tiny team in its foreground; the wall is plainly built from many separate blocks.|H1 and the six workers retain their geography beside the wall.

4|HOOK|medium|One worker tries the wall-side block with both hands, fails, and looks up; a measured pull-back explains why one person's strength is insufficient.|H1 has not lifted; red worker stays left of it.

5|HOOK_EXAMPLES|wide montage|Use distinct establishing cuts to a Greek colonnade, an Egyptian statue and a British standing stone as each object is named; retain the same drawing language.|Separate locations are explicit examples, never parts of the same worksite.

6|HOOK|medium push-in|Return to the red worker studying the block's contact with the ground; a foreman crouches to inspect the gap instead of speaking.|H1 stays grounded; foreman kneels screen-left, six-worker team visible.

8|HOOK|wide|The team stops futile pushing; the foreman lays a long wooden beam beside a solid stone fulcrum already carried in by two workers.|Beam and fulcrum lie on the ground at H1's left edge; nothing is yet lifted.

10|HOOK|medium tracking|Reveal additional workers arriving from the established path, carrying boards and rope; the original six remain identifiable.|New workers enter visibly; H1, beam and fulcrum keep their positions.

12|HOOK|close detail sequence|A worker studies the contact point, another measures the beam's long arm with a cord, and the foreman positions the fulcrum; each purposeful action matches the named skill.|Fulcrum seated firmly; beam tip not yet loaded; cord is withdrawn visibly.

16|HOOK|medium|Workers inspect H1's ground contact and compare their direct effort with the prepared long beam. Seat the fulcrum and beam without lifting yet; build toward the narrated mechanical insight.|H1 still grounded; beam seated on a firm fulcrum at its left edge; assistant holds a chock ready.

17:13|HOOK|medium to wide|As the narrator names the lever, workers lower its long arm, raise H1 only centimeters and insert a chock. Pull back as incline, friction and organization are named, revealing the prepared route and coiled rope.|H1 rests on the inserted chock; beam remains on fulcrum; rope coiled and unattached; ramp ahead screen-right.

18|ROADMAP|wide tracking|Follow one illustrative stone journey across clearly separated quarry, transport and placement stations; workers actively prepare each station instead of pointing at cards.|Overview is an explicit schematic route; no implication of instantaneous stone travel.

19|ROADMAP_QUARRY|medium|At the quarry, workers deepen a cut along a natural seam and clear loosened chips; the block remains part of the rock until the seam opens.|Q0 block partially separated at its seam; chips accumulate below.

21|ROADMAP_TRANSPORT|medium tracking|Establish a different demonstration stone already secured on a sledge; the crew pulls it screen-right across sand, then visibly prepared rollers.|Transport overview uses T0, not Q0; attached ropes and the sledge remain visible.

23|ROADMAP_LIFT|medium|A short demonstration insert shows a supported lever loading a sledge beside a wooden rope frame; operators keep hands clear of the supported load.|Distinct lifting insert; frame has visible bracing and anchors.

24|ROADMAP_RAMP|wide|Track a sledge gradually up a low earthen ramp while a rear rope team restrains rollback; finish on small lever-guided placement adjustments.|R0 reaches the upper platform on its sledge with both pulling and safety ropes attached.

27|ROADMAP_RAMP|medium pull-back|Retain R0 at the upper landing while workers make small supported placement corrections; reveal the sledge, rope, ramp and lever working as a sequence of complementary tools.|R0 seated on the prepared bed; sledge unloaded and withdrawn visibly; ramp remains present.

28|MISCONCEPTION|wide|Establish grounded D1; one person's direct pull tightens a rope but achieves no lift, while simple tools sit unused beside the crew. Reveal the tiny worker versus the stubborn mass without inventing a magic machine.|D1 grounded; rope taut to the left; tools visible on the ground.

30|MICRO_LIFT|medium|Establish the same block with two levers on visible fulcrums. Workers divide roles and insert the first beam while assistants prepare loose chocks.|D1 grounded; two beams and fulcrums in place; chocks carried by assistants.

33|MICRO_LIFT|close|Push the long arms down, raise the stone edge a few centimeters, and slide a chock into the gap; keep the opposite edge in contact with its base.|D1 partly raised and supported by first chock; beam pressure released only after support contacts stone.

36|MICRO_LIFT|medium|Reset the lever on a higher firm support, lift again, then add a second board; use real incremental motion rather than a vertical jump.|D1 supported at a second increment; old chock remains beneath it; all crew positions persist.

39|MICRO_LIFT|wide pull-back|Show the team checking each support before advancing the next increment; the camera reveals the low stepped crib supporting the full weight.|D1 rests safely on the crib; levers reset and workers wait outside the crush zone.

41|QUARRY|wide|Establish a terraced ancient quarry with attached bedrock blocks and spoil piles; workers cut trenches around a naturally bounded block.|Q1 remains attached at its base; bronze-tool crew established in an Egyptian quarry.

44|QUARRY|close|Track the trench and exposed seam as bronze tools remove small chips; emphasize separation from parent rock rather than a ready-made cube.|Q1 side trench deepened; base still attached; tools stay in workers' hands.

47|WEDGE_QUARRY|close|Cleanly establish a separate plausible wedge-splitting reconstruction. Workers hammer dry wooden wedges into a natural fissure, then pour water over them.|Q2 attached at fissure; wet wedges visibly seated in the crack; vessel held by blue worker.

48|WEDGE_QUARRY|extreme close|Show absorbed water swelling the wedge fibers and gradually widening the existing fissure; ease back as the block separates a little.|Q2 separates along the fissure; wedges stay lodged; fragments remain on quarry floor.

49|WEDGE_QUARRY|medium|Workers probe the opened seam and carefully remove loose chips, showing that material knowledge and a useful fracture plane govern the result.|Q2 separated and stationary; opened seam persists and no finished shape is implied.

52|THERMAL_QUARRY|wide to close|In a distinct non-specific quarry reconstruction, heat a small exposed seam, remove embers, then pour water; show a localized irregular crack and workers keeping back.|Separate Q3 thermal example, not a continuation of Q2; cracked stone remains grounded.

54|THERMAL_QUARRY|medium|Inspect the irregular crack from a safe distance and reject a loose fragment; communicate uncertain control instead of a perfect universal cutting technique.|Q3 imperfectly cracked; safe perimeter maintained; no cultures or tools mixed.

55|QUARRY_SHAPING|medium|At an Egyptian quarry, workers rough-dress a separated limestone block with plausible period tools; chips fall and visibly reduce its unwanted outer bulk.|Q4 separated, rough corners removed; chips accumulate where struck.

58|QUARRY_SHAPING|close tracking|Follow chisel impacts removing excess stone; pull back to a rough column or statue blank still resting on the quarry bed, already lighter for transport.|Q4 remains a rough blank on supports, not a magically finished sculpture.

61|LEVER|wide|Establish D2, a grounded demonstration block, and a long timber. A worker's bare-handed lift fails, then the foreman brings the timber to the near edge.|D2 grounded; beam brought in from left; fulcrum carried by blue worker.

64|LEVER|close|Place the beam, then seat a solid fulcrum beneath it and position hands on the long arm as board, support and force are named.|D2 grounded; fulcrum firmly seated near the load; long arm extends screen-left.

68|LEVER|medium|Several workers press the long arm down; rotate the beam about its fixed fulcrum and raise just one edge of D2, visibly exchanging distance for force.|D2 edge lifted a few centimeters; red worker operates long arm; blue assistant waits with a chock.

70|LEVER|close|Hold the tiny opening, slide a board beneath the load and transfer the weight onto it; do not increase the rise merely because the camera is closer.|D2 supported on the first board; beam unloaded only after contact is established.

73|LEVER|medium tracking|Reset the beam on a slightly higher support and perform another small lift with the existing board still in place.|D2 now rests on two incremental boards; previous supports persist.

75|LEVER|wide|Show several patient, visibly separated lever cycles with chocks inserted after each; each cycle advances only a small amount.|D2 on a low stable crib; red lever operator and blue chock handler keep their jobs.

77|LEVER_CYCLE|medium|Establish a more detailed same-method demonstration with three identifiable workers inserting long beams under grounded D3.|D3 grounded; red and ochre workers on beam ends; blue assistant beside the open edge.

79|LEVER_CYCLE|close|Workers push down together; D3 rises two centimeters around its far edge, and the blue assistant slides wooden packing into the real gap.|D3 supported on packing; fulcrums remain under both beams.

82|LEVER_CYCLE|medium|With the load supported, withdraw and visibly reposition the beams, lift another increment, then add packing without removing earlier boards.|D3 on a higher crib; all inserted packing remains and load never floats.

85|LEVER_CYCLE|wide|Use a motivated elapsed-time dissolve after a completed support cycle; show the crew finishing the crib and visibly sliding a sledge below the safely supported block.|D3 transferred onto wooden sledge S3; crib is unloaded and removed by workers.

86|SLEDGE|medium|Track around D3 on S3 to reveal two continuous runners; establish an adjacent separate rough block digging into earth in a small comparative insert.|D3 remains on S3; comparison block is explicitly separate and never swaps identity.

88|SLEDGE|close tracking|Contrast earth piling against the bare comparison stone with runners spreading D3's load. Workers secure D3 to S3 using a visible rope cradle.|D3 tied onto S3 with fixed rope cradle; hauling rope attaches to front crossbar.

90|SLEDGE|medium|The same crew leans into the taut hauling rope and slowly moves S3 screen-right; runners scrape rather than make the stone glide freely.|D3 secured on S3; rope stays anchored at front crossbar; movement rightward.

94|SURFACE_FRICTION|close|Keep S3 moving with effort on a prepared track; a worker moistens a short patch ahead and the runners cross it with reduced but still obvious resistance.|D3 and S3 remain together; damp patch stays behind after passage; no universal oil claim is illustrated.

95|EGYPT_WET_SAND|wide to close|Establish Ancient Egypt anew: a statue lashed onto ES1 plows a dry sand ridge. As the narrator describes the liquid, the carrier pours measured water ahead of the runners; hold close on the compacting strip through the brief discussion phrase.|Statue stays on ES1; same rope cradle and rightward direction; dry mound and damp strip persist; water applied before runners arrive.

97|EGYPT_WET_SAND|medium tracking|At the same pulling effort, ES1 crosses the compact damp strip more smoothly but slowly; workers still lean and brace their feet.|ES1 continues rightward; statue and attachments unchanged; no frictionless glide.

98|EGYPT_WET_SAND|close pull-back|Follow the runner contact patch, then reveal the water carrier maintaining the strip ahead while the hauling crew preserves rhythm.|Same Egyptian team, damp track and secured statue continue without a scene reset.

100|ROLLERS|wide|Establish a separate generic ancient transport reconstruction: workers lever up the sledge edge, insert the first logs and lower the runners into contact.|D4 on S4; three placed rollers contact runners and firm ground; two spare logs lie ahead.

101|ROLLERS|medium tracking|Pull S4 screen-right over the logs; show rollers rotating in contact with the prepared road and the rear log gradually emerging.|D4 secured to S4; rear roller nearly free; front spare remains carried by blue worker.

102|ROLLERS|medium|Once the rear roller clears S4, two workers lift it, carry it around the visible near side and place it in front; S4 pauses during handling.|Freed roller visibly relocated to front; no log duplicates; S4 direction remains rightward.

104|ROLLERS|wide tracking|Resume the pull and repeat one complete rear-to-front roller cycle, making continuous transport possible without an endless spawning supply.|Same three rollers recycle; D4 remains secured to S4; crew count stays six.

106|ROLLERS_RISK|close|In a separate cautionary reconstruction, a roller sinks slightly into soft ground and begins to skew; workers stop and chock the stationary sledge immediately.|D5 on S5, skewed roller still present, load chocked; no injury or runaway action.

108|COORDINATION|wide|Return to a safe firm-road team. Reveal rope handlers, roller carriers, a path preparer and the foreman, each actively performing the narrated job.|D4/S4 stopped safely; each recognizable worker has an established position and tool.

111|COORDINATION|medium tracking|Follow the roller carriers to the front, the foreman's clear stop/go hand signal, and the path worker leveling the next section; keep the load stopped during setup.|D4/S4 supported; all rollers accounted for; foreman at the road's near side.

114|COORDINATION|wide|Show a separate brief comparison: uncoordinated rope directions cancel motion, then cut to the organized crew taking the strain together.|Comparison clearly separate; main D4/S4 team remains organized and right-facing.

116|COORDINATION|wide tracking|On the foreman's single signal, the hauling line leans and steps together while rollers and guide ropes are managed in their established positions.|D4/S4 advances rightward under synchronized traction; no worker teleports across the load.

117|ANIMAL_TRACTION|wide|Establish a classical road with a harnessed ox pair slowly drawing a secured sledge; the human handler walks beside the yoke and keeps a clear route.|A1/S6 travels rightward on a road; oxen stay ahead and harness remains taut.

119|HUMAN_PRECISION|medium|Clean cut to human workers maneuvering a different block beside a narrow platform; they maintain rope angle, obey a stop signal and approach with a small lever.|D6 remains on its sledge; animals are absent from this newly established operation.

122|HUMAN_PRECISION|close|The guide holds the rope at a useful angle, the team stops, and the lever operator raises one edge only enough for a blue assistant to insert a wedge.|D6 temporarily supported on wedge; sledge still underneath; hauling rope stays fixed.

125|ANIMAL_HUMAN_COMPARE|wide then medium|Cut from a distinct ox-drawn long road haul to human centimeter corrections at the platform, establishing each location before comparing their tasks.|Two explicit examples, no sudden animal or crew replacement within one operation.

127|RAMP|wide|Establish D7/S7 at the foot of a raised stone platform; reveal the vertical height gap and the long low-angle earth ramp that provides a route.|D7 on S7 at ramp foot; pulling team ahead, safety team behind, all ropes attached.

130|RAMP|wide pan|Pan along the ramp from packed base to its broad upper landing; shovelers tamp the sides and clear the hauling lane before movement.|Ramp continuous and compact; D7/S7 still at the foot with both rope systems attached.

132|RAMP|medium tracking|The front crew pulls S7 gradually uphill while rear workers pay out the safety rope under control; load remains on its runners against the ramp.|D7/S7 a short way up ramp; rope paths remain outside workers and stone.

134|RAMP|wide explanatory|Use a clean overlay diagram beside the live ramp to compare a steep short route with a longer shallow route; show reduced pull distance-per-height tradeoff without making mass shrink.|Live D7/S7 stays on the shallow ramp; diagram is illustrative, not a second physical stone.

136|RAMP|wide tracking|Follow the slow longer haul; feet brace, taut ropes transmit effort, and the same elevation is gained through much greater travel distance.|D7/S7 halfway up; safety line still tensioned and ramp remains fully present.

138|RAMP_VARIANTS|wide comparison|Use separate, clearly framed reconstruction views of a straight ramp, a side ramp and a wrapping ramp; present layouts as possible alternatives, never a certified pyramid blueprint.|Each ramp alternative is a separate reconstruction; no same-load geography is implied.

142|RAMP_VARIANTS|close then wide|Show workers layering earth, rubble and mudbrick in one plausible ramp reconstruction, compacting each layer under a timber surface.|Layered demonstration ramp completed locally; no mixed-era machinery or materials.

143|RAMP_TOP|medium|Establish a sledge reaching its broad top landing, chock it, then lever the block onto its prepared bed. Only after seating it do workers remove a small section of ramp edge.|D8 seated on its foundation; unloaded sledge withdrawn visibly; ramp partly retained.

144|TEMPORARY_WORKS|wide pull-back|Pull back from a modest rising monument to reveal the much larger temporary earth ramp and workers still building its embankment.|Permanent structure and temporary ramp remain separate and geographically coherent.

148|TEMPORARY_WORKS|wide tracking|Follow carpenters building a platform and shovelers strengthening an approach before a hauling crew is allowed onto it.|Work platform and prepared approach completed before load arrival; no tools appear from nowhere.

151|STEP_PLATFORM|medium|Establish D9 on a low crib beside an unfinished platform; workers build the next low masonry step and bring beams and chocks into view.|D9 supported on existing crib; new step assembled adjacent, not beneath a floating load.

153|STEP_PLATFORM|close to medium|Use a fixed fulcrum to raise one edge, insert packing and transfer D9 onto the next support; repeat once as construction grows around its slow climb.|D9 rests one stage higher; all lower supports remain load-bearing until explicitly unloaded.

156|STEP_PLATFORM|wide pull-back|Reveal scaffold and masonry rising around D9's route; an elapsed-time transition occurs only after a completed supported stage.|D9 safely supported at a new construction level; stage change visibly signals elapsed time.

158|ROPE_MAKING|close|Hands twist plant fibers into strands, lay strands into a thicker rope and test its tension between a timber peg and a workbench.|R1 rope fabricated visibly; flax/hemp/palm examples shown separately, not all claimed for one culture.

161|ROPE_MAKING|close tracking|Track three short material samples into a single completed rope coil; workers inspect the fibers and tie a recognizable knot around a timber crossbar.|R1 coil and fixed knot remain visible; demonstration is material comparison, not an exact universal recipe.

162|ROPE_SAFETY|wide|Establish D10/S10 on a gentle incline with one forward traction line, side guide ropes and a separately anchored rear restraint line.|D10 on S10 chocked on incline; front, side and rear ropes have visible separate anchors.

164|ROPE_SAFETY|medium|The front crew takes tension while the rear crew pays out restraint rope around a fixed timber post; remove the chock only after both lines are controlled.|D10/S10 advances slowly uphill; rear safety line remains taut and secured.

166|ROPE_FRAME|medium|Show side guides keeping a different supported load centered, then a controlled descent through a visibly braced timber frame; operators lower the rope hand over hand.|D11 lowered a small distance onto a crib; frame, guides and rope bends stay physically legible.

169|PULLEY_COMPOUND|wide then close|Establish a later classical compound rig with one fixed and one movable pulley. As multiple sheaves are named, trace the fixed rope end and two load-supporting legs; haul extra rope for a small controlled rise.|P2 movable pulley attached to load sling; fixed end anchored above; load slightly raised under two supporting rope legs.

170|PULLEY_SINGLE|wide then close|Establish a distinct single-pulley example: one sheave fixed to a braced overhead beam, rope passing over it to a modest load and free end held by the operator.|P1 frame grounded and braced; fixed pulley above supported load; free rope end held by operator.

171|PULLEY_SINGLE|medium|The operator pulls the free end down; the pulley turns and the modest load rises slowly the same distance, showing direction change without claiming force multiplication.|P1 load a short distance off its crib; single pulley remains fixed, rope taut on both sides.

173|PULLEY_COMPOUND|close pull-back|Clean cut to an explicitly different rig with one fixed and one movable block; show the load shared by two rope legs and twice as much free rope hauled for a small rise.|P2 movable pulley attached to load sling; fixed end and supporting rope legs fully visible.

174|CLASSICAL_CRANE|wide|Establish a Greek temple worksite with a guyed wooden lifting mast, rope drum and supported sheaves; workers ready a modest column drum in a secure sling.|C1 drum grounded below braced wooden crane; rigging anchored outside the hauling crew.

177|CLASSICAL_CRANE|medium tracking|Workers rotate a capstan, rope visibly winds onto its drum and C1 slowly rises; camera follows the rope path from drum through supported pulleys to sling.|C1 suspended low in secure sling; capstan, anchored mast and rope path remain consistent.

178|CLASSICAL_CRANE|wide|Track C1 toward its prepared landing; background shows separate small port and building lifts through an explicit location-change montage, with plausible wooden rigs.|Each new location is separately established; no giant monolith or modern crane appears.

179|CLASSICAL_TOOLKIT|medium|At the Greek site, crane operators stop the modest load on supports while nearby workers use a lever and a separate sledge, showing complementary tools.|C1 supported; crane rope still attached; separate sledge load clearly distinct.

182|OBELISK|wide|Establish a plausible Egyptian raising reconstruction: O1 lies horizontal on supports beside a prepared socket, earthwork and several anchored control ropes.|O1 horizontal; butt end close to socket lip; top points screen-left; six named Egyptian workers established.

184|OBELISK|close tracking|Track from O1's lower end to the empty socket and packing earth; workers check the pivot edge and clear the exclusion zone.|O1 still horizontal; prepared socket open; ropes remain slack but attached at established points.

186|OBELISK|medium|Use levers and short support increments to start tilting O1; its lower end approaches the socket while timber cribbing supports the rising shaft.|O1 slightly inclined and fully supported; lower end at socket mouth; top moving upward, not translating vertically.

188|OBELISK|wide|Pull control ropes as the monolith pivots slowly; assistants add earth and packing under the shaft without standing underneath it.|O1 roughly halfway upright; butt entering socket; control ropes lead to visible anchors.

189|OBELISK|wide tracking|Continue the same pivot from its existing angle: the butt seats deeper and the top rises gradually. Counter-ropes check the final rotation as the shaft approaches vertical.|O1 upright in socket with temporary braces and all control ropes still attached.

190|OBELISK|medium pull-back|Workers secure braces, inspect the base and maintain rope tension before anyone approaches; show the completed controlled placement without a celebratory unsafe release.|O1 braced upright and stationary; anchors and safety perimeter persist.

192|GEOMETRY_RECAP|wide explanatory|In a neutral diagram layout, show separate small demonstrations of rolling, pivoting and supported transfer as those verbs arrive; avoid a single stone changing mechanism instantly.|Each mechanism occupies its own explicit vignette with its own load identity.

195|GEOMETRY_RECAP|medium|Continue with separately established support insertion, travel onto an earth ramp and controlled lowering into a prepared socket; all contacts remain visible.|No continuity asserted between vignettes; each load ends supported.

199|ROUTE_PREP|wide tracking|Establish an untouched route between quarry and worksite; surveyors walk it with measuring cord while the hauling block remains parked at the quarry.|D12/S12 parked left; survey team advances along the future route screen-right.

201|ROUTE_PREP|medium tracking|Workers flatten bumps, compact soft ground and remove a visible obstruction; each cleared object is carried to a spoil pile.|Route progressively level; D12/S12 still parked; spoil pile grows off the hauling lane.

205|ROUTE_PREP|medium|Lay timber on a prepared section, spread gravel and compact the next patch; carry materials in visibly rather than spawning a complete road.|Continuous prepared route extends rightward; workers finish the load-bearing surface.

208|ROUTE_PREP|wide|Return along the completed approach to the waiting sledge; the foreman checks the ground before signaling the hauling team forward.|D12/S12 enters the prepared route with fixed ropes, moving rightward.

210|ROAD_COMPARISON|medium split diagram|Compare two separate matched sledge demonstrations: the poor surface ruts and stops its load, while the prepared firm route permits a slow controlled pull.|Two distinct loads in an explicit comparison; neither changes mass or teleports.

212|EXPERIMENT|wide|Establish a modern experimental reconstruction with the same 2D stick style and simple ordinary clothing, hand-built ancient-style tools, and no powered equipment.|Modern test setting explicitly distinct from historical scenes; experimental load X1 on a sledge.

214|EXPERIMENT|medium tracking|Follow X1 through visible route preparation, measured wetting and coordinated pulling; the result comes from the prepared system rather than a secret machine.|X1 remains on the same sledge; wet track and manual tools persist.

218|HAZARD|wide|Establish a separate cautionary worksite with a chocked sledge, worn rope sample, split spare roller and a foreman inspecting the setup.|H2 load safely chocked; suspect components displayed beside it, not carrying live weight.

220|HAZARD|close insert sequence|Demonstrate frayed fibers parting on a small unloaded sample, a block edge shifting against a backup stop, and a loose wedge slipping into an empty clearance zone.|Safety examples are separate controlled tests; H2 remains chocked and nobody is under a load.

223|HAZARD|medium|A spare roller cracks under a small test load; the foreman stops an approaching worker before the crush zone and orders the live crew to wait with a clear hand signal.|H2 still immobile; cracked roller stays in the reject pile; crew safely outside danger area.

226|HAZARD_INSPECTION|medium tracking|An experienced worker checks foundation contact, judges the slope and counts available rope handlers before permitting any movement.|Load remains stopped; inspected ground, ropes and crew positions remain visible.

229|HAZARD_INSPECTION|close|Inspect an excessively steep test ramp, the worn rope and an unevenly seated block; reject the rope and insert a firm packing piece before a go signal.|Defects corrected visibly; discarded rope carried away, replacement carried in and tied before hauling.

234|BLOCK_SIZE|wide|Establish a quarry planner comparing one enormous rock blank with several manageable blocks marked only by chalk-free cut grooves; crews prepare the smaller pieces.|Distinct blanks remain grounded; no completed blocks appear without cutting.

236|BLOCK_SIZE|medium tracking|Move several moderate blocks one at a time on the same adequately sized sledge; show a practical repeated transport cycle with explicit elapsed-time cuts.|Each block has its own identity; sledge unloads before the next block is loaded.

238|MONOLITH_VALUE|wide|Establish a separate ceremonial monolith beside its intended socket; workers measure its base and prepare a larger approach to match the symbolic ambition.|V1 monolith grounded and route under preparation; no unsupported lift.

243|CULTURE_SCALE|wide montage|Establish Egypt, prehistoric Britain, a Roman temple, a Greek colonnade and a medieval cathedral in separate shots; in each, show the relevant crew doing a specific feasible stone task.|Civilizations separated by clean establishing cuts; architecture and costumes never combine.

245|KNOWN_MECHANICS|medium|At a neutral demonstration yard, a worker opens an empty equipment shelter and turns instead to the visible lever, sledge and prepared ramp; no alien or lost-machine fantasy is depicted.|All tools visible on the ground; demonstration load K1 remains supported.

247|KNOWN_MECHANICS|close sequence|Follow a lever rotating on its fulcrum, a sledge pulled up a shallow ramp and logs turning below a separately established load, timed to the named tools.|Each miniature has its own load; no shared stone changes rigs between cuts.

251|KNOWN_MECHANICS|close sequence|Show taut rope, a supported pulley, capstan rope winding, then compacted ramp earth; camera moves only when the narrated tool changes.|Supported pulley and capstan belong to one plausible classical rig; ramp insert is separate.

255|KNOWN_MECHANICS|medium|Workers check a stone with a wooden template and measuring cord, then the hauling line pulls together on a signal.|K1 supported for measurement; main pull happens only after measuring tools are removed.

259|METHOD_UNCERTAINTY|wide diagram|Present two separate plausible ramp layouts beside the same small monument outline, then return to the shared basic lever-and-rope principles; do not certify either reconstruction.|Alternative methods stay in separate diagram panels; no invented exact historical blueprint.

264|PRECISION|medium|Establish F1 delivered on a sledge beside a prepared wall bed; the crew checks a small alignment gap before touching the stone.|F1 secured on sledge, adjacent to bed; guide cord already fixed beyond working hands.

267|PRECISION_EXAMPLES|close montage|Use clearly separate wall-block, column-drum and lintel examples; show flat bedding contact, matching drum centers and a beam supported at both ends.|Examples explicitly separate; each element already safely supported before close inspection.

270|PRECISION|close|Return to F1; a lever on a firm fulcrum rotates one corner centimeters while an assistant adds a wedge and corrects the bedding.|F1 partially transferred onto bed, sledge still supporting remainder; wedge carries the lifted corner.

273|PRECISION|close tracking|Add a small amount of bedding under one side, tap the wedge, check against the taut guide cord and lower the edge into full contact.|F1 settles onto its bed; guide cord stays outside the stone; unloaded sledge withdrawn visibly.

277|PRECISION|wide to close|Pull back to the apparently massive wall, then push into F1's tiny final adjustment and full bearing contact, contrasting scale with precision.|F1 seated and aligned; tools and wedges removed only after weight transfer is complete.

280|FOREMAN|medium|Establish a foreman overseeing a fresh haul; he positions rope handlers with clear hand gestures, then gives one start and one stop signal.|D13/S13 advances a short distance and stops; foreman remains on near side, not in load path.

285|FOREMAN|wide tracking|Follow the foreman checking a ramp gradient, ordering extra packing on a weak patch and inspecting the number of properly anchored ropes.|D13/S13 stationary during inspection; additional packing and rope carried in visibly.

288|FOREMAN|wide|Show the foreman selecting the next block from an orderly staging area; a runner relays a hand signal to the far hauling crew, who wait for coordination.|Block order shown through physical staging, without invented readable plans or labels.

291|CRAFT_NETWORK|wide tracking|Track across a quarry mason, carpenter and rope maker in connected work areas; each hands a useful object or material onward to the next trade.|Objects visibly passed between workers; tools stay at their relevant stations.

294|CRAFT_NETWORK|medium tracking|Masons dress stone, carpenters finish runners, rope makers twist strands and a surveyor checks a cord while the foreman coordinates the haul.|Each craft has distinct identity and work position; no slave-status claim implied by costume.

299|CRAFT_NETWORK|wide|Quarry and soil specialists inspect the approach while the hauling leader tests rope tension; the whole team waits for the coordinated go signal.|All specialist positions established; the load remains secured and supported.

303|SHARED_PHYSICS|wide comparison|Place separate Egyptian, Greek and Andean lever reconstructions in clearly bounded sequential views; each beam pivots on a visible fulcrum to make a small supported lift.|Different crews, materials and architecture remain separate; same physics, not claimed cultural transmission.

306|SHARED_PHYSICS|medium|Return to a neutral worksite where a longer lever and more workers move a load incrementally along a prepared route; no motor or supernatural effect appears.|D14 on sledge moves slowly rightward with manual control and visible supports.

308|JOURNEY|wide|Establish one continuous classical construction geography: quarry left, prepared road center, low ramp right and upper platform beyond it; introduce a distinctive chipped-corner block J1.|J1 attached in quarry; future sledge JS1, ropes and timber supports visible in staging area; six identifiable workers.
